title: The new tax plan that could stop Social Security cuts
text:

 Medora Lee USA TODAY Updated Nov. 17, 2026, 1:07 p.m. ET Hear this story When it comes to solving Social Security's woes, show me the money, not just the people, the AARP Public Policy Institute says.
 Shifting income patterns, not just demographics, have severely damaged the program's finances over the years, wrote Richard Johnson, vice president of financial security at the nonprofit, nonpartisan research organization, in an analysis. More income now falls above the payroll tax cap or is distributed through "pass-through entities" that bypass Social Security tax, he said.
 Capital income, such as corporate profits and investment returns, has also grown faster than labor income.
 All of those can bypass Social Security payroll tax, shrinking in 2025 the share of GDP subject to Social Security payroll tax to 34%, Johnson said. That's down from 41% in 1983, Johnson said. He estimates that if Social Security’s payroll tax base had remained at 41% of GDP, full benefits could have been paid until 2059, instead of the current projection of 2032.
 “These trends have received relatively little attention in the ongoing Social Security debate,” Johnson said.
 USA TODAY Shopping: Shop sales in tech, home, fashion, beauty & more curated by our editors. What is Social Security's funding gap?
 The trust fund that supplements incoming payroll taxes to pay monthly Social Security benefits is projected to be depleted in 2032, which would force an immediate across-the-board 22% benefits cut, the latest Board of Trustees report said.
 For the past 16 years, the cost of Social Security’s retirement program has exceeded the amount it receives from taxes collected from paychecks, forcing it to dip into its trust fund reserves to cover the shortfall. Last year, the trust fund was forecast to run out in 2033.
 Then, in August, the date was moved up to the end of 2032 because of tax provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that passed in July 2025.
 How has income shifted to widen the gap?
 Workers have seen their compensation shrink as an overall part of GDP as business profits soared, Johnson said. Between 1970 and 2023, labor compensation’s share of GDP fell to 57% from 65%, with a corresponding increase in the share from corporate and investment profits. Corporate profits and investment returns aren't subject to payroll tax and don't contribute to Social Security.
 The rise in pass-through entities also has reduced Social Security revenue, Johnson said. Pass-through entities allow owners to report business profits instead of salaries on their personal income tax forms, which reduces the payroll taxes they pay and lowers their overall tax liability, he wrote.
 The growth in pass-throughs may account for as much as a third of the recent, Johnson said.
 How can the funding gap be filled?
 With a looming shortfall less than six years away and a class of new U.S. senators on the watch starting in January, Americans hope a Social Security fix becomes a top priority.
 Many new senators elected in the blue wave midterm have said they support raising or removing the payroll tax wage cap but didn't always provide details. Raising or eliminating the cap would mean high earners pay more into the program. Currently, only salaries and wages up to $184,500 in 2026 are subject to the payroll tax.
 In 2027, that threshold, adjusted annually for inflation, rises to $192,300.
 But changes to the cap won't be enough. Using 2025 data, Social Security's trustees said eliminating the payroll tax wage cap to include all wages would only fund the trust for three years before returning to a shortfall and requiring additional new taxes or benefit changes.
 That's why AARP also focuses on bringing in other revenue, such as a new tax on investment income. Social Security trustees project a new 12.4% tax on investment income earned by officers and limited partners through pass-through entities would hit only higher earners and close about a quarter of Social Security’s 75-year financing gap.
 Taxpayers with annual incomes of $1 million or more represent only 1% of filers, but they receive 48% of all investment income, defined as interest, dividends, rent, business income, farm income, and payments from pass-through entities, estates and trusts, as well as the sale of capital assets, Johnson said. Those who earn between $500,000 and $999,999 are another 1% of taxpayers and receive 12% of investment income.
 Independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who becomes the Senate's Social Security subcommittee chair in January, said he wants to scrap the payroll cap above $250,000 and tax business and investment income. Social Security would be so flush with cash that the government could even raise benefits by $2,400 annually, he said.
 Some economists, however, have been critical of such plans. More taxes would disincentivize work and investments and punish small- and medium-sized businesses, they said.
 "While 'fair share' tax increases will remain a regular applause line in Democratic (and even some Republican) circles, recent history suggests no plausible path for the substantial tax increases necessary to close the Social Security and Medicare shortfalls without also significantly reforming benefits," center-left researcher Brookings said in an analysis. "Realistically, a tax-only solution to closing long-term Social Security...shortfalls would require significant middle-class tax increases."
 Curbing benefits for high-earners could help, some economists said. For those who can live comfortably on their own savings, politicians might consider trimming or capping their benefits, eliminating their annual cost-of-living adjustment , putting their benefits on a sliding scale so that benefits decrease as income rises, or taxing 100% of their Social Security benefits, Brookings said . Currently, up to 85% of everyone's Social Security is taxed based on income levels.
 Virginia Democrat Sen. Tim Kaine and Louisiana Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy propose to borrow $1.5 trillionfrom the government to create a separate fund to invest in stocks, bonds, and other high-return assets for 75 years in parallel with the current Social Security fund. Cassidy is pushing the plan to be heard on the Senate floor before year-end.
 Alicia Munnell, senior adviser at the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College, pushed back, noting the plan would require more borrowing for the investment fund in addition to borrowing to fund the actual Social Security in parallel.
